entries.definition: A writer’s specific word choices, considered for precision, connotation, and formality.
entries.example: Choosing “slender” rather than “skinny” or “scrawny.”
entries.analysis: Shapes how a subject is evaluated and signals the writer’s attitude before any argument is made explicit.

entries.definition: The arrangement of words and the construction of sentences (length, order, fragmentation).
entries.example: A clipped sentence after a long one: “She had planned every detail for months. It collapsed in an hour.”
entries.analysis: Controls pace and emphasis; abrupt syntax can convey tension or a sense of finality that the words alone don’t carry.

entries.definition: The level of formality and variety of language appropriate to a context or audience.
entries.example: “We regret to inform you” (formal) vs. “Sorry, bad news” (informal).
entries.analysis: Shapes the relationship with the audience, suggesting authority, closeness or shared values.

entries.definition: The writer’s attitude toward the subject or audience, conveyed through diction and style.
entries.example: A review calling a blockbuster “competent, inoffensive, and instantly forgettable.”
entries.analysis: Helps establish an attitude toward the subject or audience. Explain which words support that attitude and whether it changes.

entries.definition: The emotional quality a text creates for the reader.
entries.example: Long shadows, a ticking clock, an empty corridor.
entries.analysis: Can make a scene feel uneasy, comic, peaceful or otherwise distinctive. Connect the atmosphere to specific details; readers may respond differently.

entries.definition: The associations and emotional overtones a word carries beyond its literal meaning.
entries.example: “Home” often suggests belonging; “house” may emphasize the building. Context can make either word comforting or unsettling.
entries.analysis: Lets a writer suggest an attitude through a word’s associations, even when the statement appears neutral.

entries.definition: The literal, dictionary meaning of a word.
entries.example: “Snake” denotes a legless reptile.
entries.analysis: Gives a starting point for comparing what a word literally means with the associations it carries.

entries.definition: Informal, conversational language, including slang and regional usage.
entries.example: “gonna,” “y’all,” “it’s no biggie.”
entries.analysis: Can suggest familiarity, shared identity or a speaker’s background. In another context, it may sound affected or inappropriate. Explain why the wording fits this situation.

entries.definition: A mild or indirect expression substituted for one considered harsh or blunt.
entries.example: “Collateral damage” for civilian deaths; “let go” for fired.
entries.analysis: Softens or hides uncomfortable realities. Ask what the wording avoids naming and whose interests that serves.

entries.definition: Descriptive language appealing to the senses (sight, sound, touch, taste, smell).
entries.example: “The rain hissed on the hot pavement.”
entries.analysis: Makes experience vivid and immediate, drawing the reader into the text’s world and reinforcing mood.

entries.definition: An implicit comparison stating that one thing is another.
entries.example: “The classroom was a zoo.”
entries.analysis: Compresses complex meaning into a single image and invites the reader to transfer the qualities of one thing onto another.

entries.definition: An explicit comparison using “like” or “as.”
entries.example: “Her stare was like cold water.”
entries.analysis: Clarifies or intensifies a quality while keeping the two terms distinct, often making the unfamiliar accessible.

entries.definition: Attributing human qualities to non-human things or abstractions.
entries.example: “The wind clawed at the windows.”
entries.analysis: Makes non-human things seem alive and can connect the surroundings with a character’s feelings.

entries.definition: Referring to something by the name of an associated thing.
entries.example: “The Crown” for the monarchy; “the White House said.”
entries.analysis: Compresses an institution or concept into a concrete emblem, shaping how power or authority is perceived.

entries.definition: A part stands for the whole, or the whole for a part.
entries.example: “All hands on deck”; “wheels” for a car.
entries.analysis: Focuses attention on a telling detail and can reduce or elevate its subject through that selective framing.

entries.definition: Using an object, image, or action to represent a larger idea.
entries.example: A recurring caged bird representing confinement.
entries.analysis: Look for details that support a meaning beyond the literal object. A familiar association is a starting point, not a fixed answer; context can change it.

entries.definition: A recurring image, idea, or structure that develops a theme.
entries.example: Repeated references to hands throughout a novel.
entries.analysis: Repetition draws attention to a detail or idea. Track what changes each time it appears and how the pattern contributes to the text.

entries.definition: A reference to another text, person, event, or work.
entries.example: Calling an ambition “his Icarus moment.”
entries.analysis: Borrows the weight and associations of the referenced source, enriching meaning for readers who recognize it.

entries.definition: Projecting human emotion onto nature or weather.
entries.example: A storm breaking as a character’s marriage collapses.
entries.analysis: Makes emotional conflict visible through the natural world, connecting changes in the surroundings with changes in feeling.

entries.definition: Repetition of initial consonant sounds in nearby words.
entries.example: “a sudden, sickening silence.”
entries.analysis: Draws the ear to a phrase, creating emphasis, rhythm, or memorability—common in slogans and headlines.

entries.definition: Repetition of vowel sounds within nearby words.
entries.example: “the light of the fire is a sight.”
entries.analysis: Creates internal musicality and can smooth or slow a line, binding words together by sound.

entries.definition: Repetition of “s,” “sh,” or soft “c” sounds.
entries.example: “the soft hiss of the simmering surf.”
entries.analysis: Produces a hushed, soothing, or sometimes sinister texture depending on context.

entries.definition: Words that imitate the sounds they describe.
entries.example: “buzz,” “crash,” “murmur.”
entries.analysis: Makes description more immediate by letting the word echo the sound it names.

entries.definition: The continuation of a phrase or sentence beyond a line break without a syntactic pause.
entries.example: “I think that I shall never see / A poem lovely as a tree.”
entries.analysis: Creates momentum and can stage a small surprise as the sense spills across the line break.

entries.definition: A deliberate pause within a line of verse.
entries.example: “To be, or not to be — that is the question.”
entries.analysis: A pause can emphasize a word or mark hesitation, reflection or a turn in thought. Explain what its placement does in this line.

entries.definition: A persuasive appeal based on the speaker’s credibility or character.
entries.example: “As a doctor with twenty years’ experience…”
entries.analysis: Invites trust by drawing on existing authority or building credibility through knowledge, honesty and attention to the audience’s concerns.

entries.definition: A persuasive appeal to the audience’s emotions.
entries.example: An image of a hungry child in a charity campaign.
entries.analysis: Name the emotion—such as protective concern, guilt or hope—and explain how particular choices create it and connect it to the request. Naming the subject alone is not enough.

entries.definition: A persuasive appeal based on logic, evidence, or reasoning.
entries.example: “Three studies confirm the policy cut accidents by 40%.”
entries.analysis: Connects evidence with a conclusion. Explain that reasoning and test its assumptions; a number alone does not make an argument logical.

entries.definition: Repetition of the same word(s) at the start of successive clauses.
entries.example: “We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds…”
entries.analysis: Builds rhythm and cumulative emphasis, lending speeches force and momentum.

entries.definition: Repeating grammatical structure across phrases or clauses.
entries.example: “Easy to learn, hard to master.”
entries.analysis: Creates balance and clarity, making ideas feel ordered, memorable, and authoritative.

entries.definition: A series of three parallel words, phrases, or clauses.
entries.example: “government of the people, by the people, for the people.”
entries.analysis: Three linked elements can build rhythm, emphasis or a sense of completion. Explain what the particular sequence adds, rather than assuming three items are always persuasive.

entries.definition: Placing contrasting ideas in parallel structure.
entries.example: “Ask not what your country can do for you—ask what you can do for your country.”
entries.analysis: A balanced contrast can make a difference clear and memorable. Identify what is opposed and why that distinction matters.

entries.definition: A question posed for effect rather than for an answer.
entries.example: “How long must we wait for change?”
entries.analysis: Guides the audience toward an answer the wording already suggests, while appearing to invite them to decide.

entries.definition: Deliberate exaggeration for emphasis or effect.
entries.example: “I’ve told you a million times.”
entries.analysis: Amplifies feeling or stakes—for emphasis, humor, or to expose intensity of attitude.

entries.definition: Understatement minimises something; litotes is a form that affirms by negating its opposite (for example, “not bad”).
entries.example: “Not bad” for excellent; “a slight inconvenience” for a disaster.
entries.analysis: Creates irony or restraint, inviting the audience to supply the fuller meaning.

entries.definition: A gap between what is said or expected and what is meant or occurs (verbal, dramatic, situational).
entries.example: A fire station burning down (situational).
entries.analysis: Examine the gap between what is said or expected and what the text reveals. Explain what the gap asks readers to question.

entries.definition: The use of irony, exaggeration, or ridicule to criticize.
entries.example: A mock ad selling “Outrage™, now in convenient daily doses.”
entries.analysis: Exposes folly or vice while entertaining, prompting the audience to judge the target.

entries.definition: Placing two elements side by side to highlight contrast or connection.
entries.example: A luxury car ad printed beside a story on poverty.
entries.analysis: Generates meaning through proximity, prompting the reader to compare and draw conclusions.

entries.definition: A compressed paradox joining contradictory terms.
entries.example: “deafening silence,” “bittersweet.”
entries.analysis: Captures complexity or tension in a phrase, making the reader hold two opposed ideas at once.

entries.definition: A statement that seems self-contradictory but reveals a truth.
entries.example: “Less is more.”
entries.analysis: Provokes thought by resisting easy resolution, often pointing to a deeper insight.

entries.definition: Hints or clues that anticipate later developments.
entries.example: An early mention of a loaded gun in a drawer.
entries.analysis: Builds suspense and coherence, rewarding rereading and shaping the reader’s expectations.

entries.definition: The vantage from which a story is told (first person, third limited, omniscient).
entries.example: An unreliable first-person narrator who misjudges events.
entries.analysis: Controls what the reader knows and trusts, shaping sympathy, irony, and access to the truth.

entries.definition: Third-person narration that blends the narrator’s voice with a character’s thoughts.
entries.example: “She would not cry. Not here, not in front of them.”
entries.analysis: Brings readers close to a character’s thoughts while keeping a third-person narrator. Differences between their voices can create irony.

entries.definition: Beginning a narrative in the middle of the action.
entries.example: Opening on a chase already underway, with context filled in later.
entries.analysis: Can create urgency or curiosity by withholding context; may also create disorientation. Consider what the reader must work out.

entries.definition: The circumstances surrounding a text’s production and reception (historical, cultural, biographical, situational).
entries.example: Reading a wartime poster in light of 1940s rationing.
entries.analysis: The time, place, audience and circumstances can change how a text is understood. Use relevant evidence rather than treating background information as a substitute for reading.

entries.definition: The shaping of a text’s meaning by its relationship to other texts.
entries.example: A film that restages the structure of a famous myth.
entries.analysis: Layers meaning through echo, homage, or parody, and positions a text within a wider conversation.

entries.definition: A text’s slant or partiality toward a particular view, often through selection and framing.
entries.example: A report quoting only one side and labeling the other “so-called experts.”
entries.analysis: Examine how selection, emphasis and assumptions favor a particular view. Bias can be explicit or can appear in an account presented as neutral.

entries.definition: The visual prominence of an element in an image or layout (size, placement, color, focus).
entries.example: A product lit and centered while the model is blurred behind it.
entries.analysis: Identify what stands out through size, contrast, placement or another choice. Explain why that detail matters; prominence does not guarantee a fixed order of attention.

entries.definition: The direction and object of looking within an image, including whether a subject looks at the viewer.
entries.example: A model staring directly out of an advertisement.
entries.analysis: Direct gaze can invite contact, challenge or pressure; looking away can draw attention elsewhere or make the viewer an observer. Expression, setting and distance help determine the relationship.

entries.definition: The way text (a caption or headline) fixes or directs (anchors) the meaning of an image.
entries.example: A neutral photo captioned “The face of a crisis.”
entries.analysis: Constrains an image’s many possible readings, steering the viewer toward a preferred interpretation.

entries.definition: The overall arrangement of visual elements within the frame.
entries.analysis: Comment on how arrangement guides the viewer's eye and creates meaning or hierarchy.

entries.definition: What is included/excluded by the image's edges; also elements within the image that enclose the subject.
entries.analysis: Examine what the image includes and leaves outside its boundaries. Explain how the visible selection shapes the subject without inventing what lies beyond the frame.

entries.definition: Placing key elements along imaginary lines that divide the frame into thirds.
entries.analysis: Consider how off-center placement relates the subject to surrounding space; it may create balance, movement or tension.

entries.definition: Lines (roads, fences, gazes) that direct attention toward a focal point.
entries.analysis: Follow where the lines lead and what they connect or emphasize. They suggest a route for attention; viewers need not follow it in one fixed order.

entries.definition: Empty or unoccupied area around the subject.
entries.analysis: Consider what the empty space does beside the subject: it may emphasize, isolate, simplify or suggest absence. Choose the reading supported by this composition.

entries.definition: The element that draws the eye first.
entries.analysis: Identify what is prioritized and how (size, color, sharpness, placement).

entries.definition: Distribution of visual weight; symmetry is mirrored, asymmetry weighted unevenly.
entries.analysis: Symmetry can suggest order or formality; asymmetry can suggest energy or unease.

entries.definition: How much of the image is in sharp focus (shallow vs. deep).
entries.analysis: Shallow focus isolates a subject; deep focus situates it within a context.

entries.definition: The areas that appear nearest to the viewer, between near and far, and furthest away.
entries.analysis: Explain how details at different distances relate to one another.

entries.definition: How much an element attracts the eye (size, color, contrast, position).
entries.analysis: Compare the weight of text vs. image, or of one figure against another.

entries.definition: Placing elements side by side to invite contrast, connection or comparison.
entries.analysis: Explore irony, contrast, or unexpected associations the pairing produces.

entries.definition: Subject seen from a distance, showing surroundings.
entries.analysis: Emphasizes environment and context over the individual.

entries.definition: Subject shown from roughly the waist up.
entries.analysis: Balances the person with some context; common for 'relatable' figures.

entries.definition: Frame filled by a face or object detail.
entries.analysis: Often invites intimacy or scrutiny of detail; the subject and context may make proximity comforting, intrusive or unsettling.

entries.definition: A very tight detail (eyes, hands, texture).
entries.analysis: A tight view can emphasize a detail or make it feel intimate, intrusive or unfamiliar. Explain what the chosen detail contributes.

entries.definition: Camera level with the subject.
entries.analysis: Often suggests equality or familiarity; expression, distance and context may still establish tension or unequal power.

entries.definition: Camera looks up at the subject.
entries.analysis: Commonly empowers the subject. Expression, setting and accompanying text may make that power heroic, threatening or ironic.

entries.definition: Camera looks down on the subject.
entries.analysis: Commonly diminishes the subject or suggests vulnerability. Check whether context instead invites affection, scrutiny or a practical overview.

entries.definition: Directly overhead perspective.
entries.analysis: Detachment, surveillance, pattern, or overwhelming scale.

entries.definition: Tilted, off-level framing.
entries.analysis: A tilted frame often suggests instability or disorientation, but may also be playful or show movement. Connect the angle to the scene.

entries.definition: The position or perspective from which we see.
entries.analysis: Ask whose eyes we are seeing through, and how that positions us.

entries.definition: The range of colors used.
entries.analysis: Describe the range of colors and connect it to the subject, wording and purpose. Green might suggest nature beside a forest or money beside banknotes; color alone does not establish either meaning.

entries.definition: Hue = the color itself; saturation = its intensity.
entries.analysis: High saturation can suggest intensity; muted color may suggest restraint, bleakness or nostalgia. Connect the palette to the subject and purpose.

entries.definition: Warm = reds, oranges, yellows; cool = blues, greens.
entries.analysis: Warm colors often suggest comfort or intensity; cool colors calm or distance. Cultural associations and surrounding details can alter these readings.

entries.definition: Degree of difference between light/dark or colors.
entries.analysis: Strong contrast can emphasize edges or differences; low contrast can soften or obscure them. Explain what is clarified or concealed here.

entries.definition: Bright, even, low-shadow lighting.
entries.analysis: Bright, even lighting can suggest openness, cheerfulness or an idealized setting. The subject and context may make that brightness feel artificial or unsettling instead.

entries.definition: Dark tones with strong shadows and selective light.
entries.analysis: Often suggests mystery, tension or intimacy. Identify what the shadows conceal or reveal and how that serves this image.

entries.definition: Strong contrasts of light and shadow that give shapes a sense of depth, a technique also used in painting.
entries.analysis: Strong light-dark contrasts can give forms depth or emphasize dramatic differences. Explain what is revealed and what remains in shadow.

entries.definition: Subject dark against a lit background.
entries.analysis: A silhouette can hide identity or emphasize a recognizable shape. Consider whether that concealment suggests mystery, anonymity or something else in context.

entries.definition: Single-color (usually black-and-white) image.
entries.analysis: Can signal the past, authenticity, starkness, or timelessness.

entries.definition: Tone is the attitude conveyed; mood is the atmosphere evoked. Lighting and color can contribute to either.
entries.analysis: Link color and lighting choices to the feeling created for the viewer.

entries.definition: Real or implied lines (including gazes and gestures) that carry the eye.
entries.analysis: Diagonals often suggest movement, horizontals stability, and verticals height or strength. Identify how the lines interact with the subject.

entries.definition: Geometric = regular, man-made; organic = natural, irregular.
entries.analysis: Geometric forms often suggest order; organic forms may suggest nature or irregularity. Their arrangement can complicate those associations.

entries.definition: Repeated visual elements.
entries.analysis: Repetition can create rhythm, emphasis, or a sense of monotony or conformity.

entries.definition: The implied surface quality (rough, smooth, soft).
entries.analysis: Surface detail can suggest touch, age or material qualities. Explain what that impression adds; roughness does not automatically make an image more truthful.

entries.definition: Relative size of elements to each other or to the viewer.
entries.analysis: Exaggerated scale can dwarf or empower; distorted proportion signals unease.

entries.definition: Techniques that create three-dimensionality (converging lines, overlap, diminishing size).
entries.analysis: Perspective positions the viewer in space and controls what feels near or far.

entries.definition: The style and arrangement of lettering.
entries.analysis: Serifs may suggest tradition, sans-serifs modernity, and script elegance or intimacy. Test these associations against the specific lettering, genre and context.

entries.definition: How text and image are arranged together on the page or screen.
entries.analysis: Analyze what sits where. Position signals importance and shapes reading order.

entries.definition: What stands out most in a text–image composition.
entries.analysis: Identify what stands out through size, contrast, placement or another choice. Explain why that detail matters; prominence does not guarantee a fixed order of attention.

entries.definition: The route the eye typically takes through the composition.
entries.analysis: Trace a plausible route using salience, placement and vectors. Explain how that sequence connects ideas; viewers need not follow one fixed path.

entries.definition: Text that accompanies and comments on an image.
entries.analysis: Ask how the caption narrows, extends or changes the image’s possible meanings. It can guide interpretation without removing every alternative.

entries.definition: Brand mark and catchphrase.
entries.analysis: Explain how the design or wording presents an identity or value. Recognition may encourage trust, skepticism or another response depending on the audience and context.

entries.definition: The literal, descriptive level: what is actually shown.
entries.analysis: Start analysis here: describe precisely before interpreting.

entries.definition: The associations and ideas an element evokes.
entries.analysis: Move from 'what is shown' to 'what it suggests': the inference that forms the basis of analysis.

entries.definition: The form (signifier) and the concept it triggers (signified).
entries.analysis: Distinguish the visible or audible sign from the idea it suggests. Explain how context supports that association rather than assigning one permanent meaning.

entries.definition: An icon resembles what it represents; an index has a direct connection to it, as smoke does to fire; a symbol depends on a learned convention, as a flag does.
entries.analysis: Ask whether a sign communicates through resemblance, a direct connection or a learned convention. Use the distinction only when it helps explain the meaning.

entries.definition: One thing presented as another to transfer meaning.
entries.analysis: Explain the comparison being made and what it implies about the subject.

entries.definition: An element that stands for an abstract idea.
entries.analysis: Look for details that support a meaning beyond the literal object. A familiar association is a starting point, not a fixed answer; context can change it.

entries.definition: Reference to or borrowing from other texts or images.
entries.analysis: Name the reference (parody, homage, allusion) and what it adds for viewers who recognize it.

entries.definition: How 'real' or truthful an image claims to be.
entries.analysis: Ask how the style claims truth or authority. A photograph may seem credible but invite distrust; a cartoon can communicate a serious argument.

entries.definition: Where figures look: at the viewer (direct / demand) or away (offer).
entries.analysis: Direct gaze can invite contact, challenge or pressure; looking away can draw attention elsewhere or make the viewer an observer. Expression, setting and distance help determine the relationship.

entries.definition: Posture, expression, and gesture of figures.
entries.analysis: Read stance and expression for attitude, power, emotion, and relationships.

entries.definition: The intended viewers, shaped by demographics and context.
entries.analysis: Infer the audience from choices in style, color, language, and imagery.

entries.definition: When, where, by whom, and under what conditions the image was made.
entries.analysis: Connect choices to the creator, medium, culture, and moment.

entries.definition: How and where audiences encounter the image.
entries.analysis: Consider how platform and setting change meaning (billboard vs. feed vs. gallery).

entries.definition: What the image is designed to do: inform, persuade, entertain, provoke, sell.
entries.analysis: Evaluate how effectively the techniques serve the purpose.

entries.definition: Appeals to credibility, emotion, and logic made visually.
entries.analysis: Explain how visual choices build credibility, invite a particular emotion or support a line of reasoning. Connect the appeals where they work together.

entries.definition: How people, groups, or ideas are depicted.
entries.analysis: Ask who is shown, how, and whose viewpoint is centered or excluded.

entries.definition: Simplified, repeated representations of types of people.
entries.analysis: Discuss whether the image reinforces or subverts the stereotype.

entries.definition: The values and assumptions encoded in an image.
entries.analysis: Uncover what the image treats as 'normal' or desirable, and who benefits.
